topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digits of Pi

outline.topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digits of Pi

sections.title: The Hook: The Pi Mystery
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive phenomenon: when two blocks of mass ratio 100^N collide (one sliding toward another stationary one), the total number of elastic collisions equals the first N+1 digits of Pi. Pose the question: 'How do mechanical collisions encode the geometry of a circle?'
sections.example: Imagine two space-faring turtles pushing blocks of mass 1kg and 100kg. As they bounce, the collision counter ticks: 3, 1, 4... Pi appears.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Conservation Laws in 2D
sections.content: Review elastic collision physics. Explain that 1D elastic collisions can be mapped to a 2D reflection problem. Use a velocity-space diagram (V-diagram) where the axes are the velocities of the two blocks. A collision is a reflection off a 'wall' defined by the mass ratio.
sections.example: Visualize the velocity state as a particle moving in a 2D plane; every collision is the particle bouncing off an angled line representing the law of conservation of momentum and energy.

sections.title: Mapping Collisions to Circular Arcs
sections.content: Show that for mass ratios of 100^N, the 'wall' reflection angle becomes increasingly constrained. Explain the transformation to polar coordinates where the path of the system's velocity becomes a sequence of chords on a circle. As the mass ratio increases, these chords approximate the circumference of a circle.
sections.example: Draw a circle segment. Instead of straight lines, use an animation showing how the 'velocity vector' trace gets closer and closer to an arc as the mass of the second block grows exponentially.

sections.title: The Geometric Proof: Why Pi?
sections.content: Connect the total number of collisions to the angle subtended by the arcs. The total angle of the path is effectively Pi radians. The number of 'ticks' corresponds to how many times the trajectory fits into that angle, which is the definition of Pi (ratio of circumference to diameter).
sections.example: An animation showing a 'collision-counter' gauge rotating like a clock hand, stopping exactly at the segment corresponding to 3.1415...

sections.title: Synthesis & Conclusion
sections.content: Summarize that Pi is not just for circles; it is a universal constant for any system undergoing periodic or bounded constraints. Encourage students to view physical interactions as geometry in disguise.
sections.example: Final shot: A digital display on a futuristic machine counting collisions as '3', '1', '4', '1', '5' while a circular orbital path is traced in the background.
